distractorExplanations.b: Clients retain the right to withdraw consent; a no-stop waiver is invalid.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent after the first exposure is not informed; the risks must be known up front.

prompt: A State A LCSW gets a Zoom request from a current private-pay client who is now on a two-week vacation in State B, where the clinician is not licensed. What is the best next step?

options.text: Confirm you may legally practice in the client's location before holding session
Proceed because a home-state clinical license follows the client on any vacation
Proceed if the client routes Zoom through a VPN that shows an in-state IP
Skip a telehealth consent addendum because video is just an office session online

explanation: Telehealth practice is generally regulated where the client is located at the time of service. Treating someone in a state where the LCSW is unlicensed (and not covered by a compact or exception) can be unlicensed practice. The clinician verifies jurisdiction, documents telehealth-specific consent, and arranges local care if the session cannot legally proceed.

distractorExplanations.b: A home-state license does not automatically travel with the client across state lines.
distractorExplanations.c: A VPN display is not a substitute for lawful licensure in the client's actual location.
distractorExplanations.d: Video adds jurisdiction, emergency, and technology risks that belong in telehealth consent, not the office form alone.

prompt: A couple you have treated jointly for six months in private practice asks you to write a custody affidavit favoring one partner. What should you do?

options.text: Write the affidavit for the partner you believe is the better parent
Decline the forensic role and consult; explain the conflict
Mail an affidavit to the court without telling the other partner
Read selected session notes in a local news interview about the case

explanation: Treating a couple and then offering forensic custody opinions for one partner is a prohibited or high-risk role conflict. The treating clinician is not a court-appointed evaluator and is not a hired advocate. Best practice is to decline, consult, explain the conflict to both clients, and refer them to an independent evaluator if the court needs an opinion.

distractorExplanations.a: Picking a "better parent" converts treatment into advocacy and harms the other client in the conjoint work.
distractorExplanations.c: A secret court filing breaches confidentiality with the other partner and still creates the dual role.
distractorExplanations.d: Public disclosure of session content is a confidentiality violation, not a custody solution.

prompt: A solo LCSW's biller suggests coding 25-minute psychotherapy visits as 90837 (60 minutes) so "the plan will actually pay." What should the clinician do?

options.text: Submit 90837 anyway because the diagnosis could have filled a longer hour
Leave coding to the biller; the clinician's license does not cover claims
Refuse and bill only the time and service that actually occurred
Bill a 45-minute code as a compromise for the 25-minute contacts

explanation: Billing for time or a procedure that was not provided is insurance fraud. The treating LCSW remains responsible for the accuracy of claims submitted under the license, even when a biller prepares the forms. Codes must match documented duration and service, not the reimbursement the practice wishes it had earned.

distractorExplanations.a: A diagnosis that "could have" justified a longer session does not license upcoding time that was not delivered.
distractorExplanations.b: Delegating claims to a biller does not shift legal responsibility off the licensee.
distractorExplanations.d: A 45-minute code for a 25-minute visit is still a false claim, just a smaller one.

prompt: A private-practice LCSW wants to advertise EMDR after a single weekend webinar, with no consultation and no supervised cases. What is required before offering it as treatment?

options.text: Begin EMDR next week based on the webinar certificate alone
Begin after reading the treatment manual cover to cover once
Begin if the client signs a consent to "try a new method"
Get training and consultation before offering EMDR

explanation: NASW 1.04 requires practice only within demonstrated competence. A new specialty modality such as EMDR needs education plus consultation or supervision until the clinician can practice safely—not a weekend badge. Clients may not consent away the competence requirement.

distractorExplanations.a: A single webinar certificate does not establish competence in a trauma-processing method.
distractorExplanations.b: Reading a manual is preparation, not supervised skill; it is not enough to advertise EMDR.
distractorExplanations.c: Informed consent cannot substitute for training; an untrained clinician still should not deliver EMDR.

prompt: A current private-practice therapy client asks the solo LCSW to become paid co-owners of a wellness-coaching LLC. What is the ethical issue?

Accept and keep separate email accounts so the roles never mix

Accept if the client agrees never to mention the business in session

explanation: NASW 1.06 cautions against dual relationships that risk exploitation or loss of professional judgment. The cleanest protection is to decline the business role while treatment continues (or end one role before starting the other, with consultation).

distractorExplanations.c: Trading fee reductions for equity is a financial dual relationship, not a safeguard.

prompt: A solo LCSW closing a private practice wants to shred adult psychotherapy charts 12 months after the last visit to save storage. What governs retention?

options.text: Shred at 12 months because a uniform national seven-year clock already ended
Keep records for the longer of state, HIPAA, and contract rules
Destroy adult charts the month the person turns 18, even if that is imminent
Use only the NASW Code's numbered retention years and ignore the state statute

explanation: Record retention is set by state licensing rules, HIPAA, and payer or malpractice-contract requirements—the clinician follows the longest applicable period, then destroys records securely. Twelve months is far too short in most jurisdictions. NASW 3.04 points to those external timelines rather than inventing a single closet-space rule.

distractorExplanations.a: There is no uniform national seven-year clock that expires at 12 months; state periods vary and are longer.
distractorExplanations.c: Age 18 is about minors' majority, not a destroy-now rule for adult charts.
distractorExplanations.d: The NASW Code does not publish a numeric retention schedule that overrides state law.

prompt: A private-pay client asks the LCSW to put "major depression, severe" on the claim so the plan will pay, though the assessment supports adjustment disorder. What should the clinician do?

options.text: Enter the requested severe-depression code because clients choose their labels
List both diagnoses and let the insurer decide which one to pay
Bill the diagnosis the assessment supports, not the code that pays more
Submit the claim with no diagnosis so the form stays value-neutral

explanation: Diagnosis on a claim must match the clinical assessment. Upcoding to a more severe, better-reimbursed disorder at the client's request is billing fraud and a falsification of the record. The ethical and legal course is to document and bill the supported diagnosis, explain coverage limits honestly, and discuss self-pay or a true appeal—not a fabricated code.

distractorExplanations.a: Clients do not get to pick reimbursable diagnoses; the clinician's assessment controls the record.
distractorExplanations.b: Listing an unsupported severe-depression code still puts a false diagnosis on the claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Payer claims generally require a diagnosis; omitting it is not a lawful workaround.

prompt: A solo LCSW wants to run ongoing psychotherapy on a consumer video app with no business associate agreement because "clients already have it." What is the best practice?

options.text: Switch to a HIPAA-capable platform with a BAA and document telehealth consent
Stay on the consumer app if clients sign a waiver of all privacy rights
Stay on the app because popular consumer video is automatically HIPAA-covered
Move the same clinical content to text on that app instead of video to cut risk

explanation: HIPAA requires appropriate safeguards for electronic PHI. Ongoing therapy on an ordinary consumer video product without a BAA (when one is required) is a security risk. Best practice is a HIPAA-capable platform with a signed BAA plus telehealth informed consent covering technology limits, emergencies, and recording—not a blanket privacy waiver.

distractorExplanations.b: Clients cannot waive the clinician's HIPAA security duties with a blanket form.
distractorExplanations.c: Consumer popularity does not equal a covered, BAA-backed telehealth platform.
distractorExplanations.d: Texting clinical content on the same unsecured app still transmits PHI without proper safeguards.
